en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 15.1 (SN 15.1, PTS SN ii 178) 1. First Chapter: On Grass and Wood **Tiṇakaṭṭhasutta – The Discourse on Grass and Wood** “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a great heap of grass and wood, and a man would come along bringing a fire-stick. He would rub it against the grass and wood, but he would not produce fire nor generate heat. Why is that? Because the grass and wood are insufficient, and the man’s effort is weak. “In the same way, bhikkhus, for one who does not possess wisdom, even though he may practice much exertion, he will not produce the fire of noble knowledge and vision; he will not generate the heat of noble knowledge and vision. Why is that? Because his wisdom is insufficient, and his exertion is weak. “But suppose, bhikkhus, there were a great heap of grass and wood, and a man would come along bringing a fire-stick. He would rub it against the grass and wood, and he would produce fire and generate heat. Why is that? Because the grass and wood are sufficient, and the man’s effort is strong. “In the same way, bhikkhus, for one who possesses wisdom, even though he may practice little exertion, he will produce the fire of noble knowledge and vision; he will generate the heat of noble knowledge and vision. Why is that? Because his wisdom is sufficient, and his exertion is strong.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.

Suppose, bhikkhus, a man would cut up whatever grass, wood, branches, and foliage there is in this Jambudīpa and collect it in a single heap; having done so, he would set aside a tally for each piece, saying:”

‘This is my mother; this is the mother of that mother of mine’—monks, the mothers of that man’s mother would not come to an end, even though the grass, wood, branches, and foliage in this Jambudīpa were to be completely exhausted and consumed. Why is that?
“Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.
So long, monks, has this suffering been experienced, so intense has it been, so much calamity has been experienced, and the charnel-ground has increased.
"To this extent, bhikkhus, it is indeed enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them.
Thus was the first [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 15.2. (SN 15.2, PTS SN ii 179)
1. First Chapter: The Discourse on the Earth.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.
Suppose, bhikkhus, that a man would reduce this great earth to balls of clay the size of jujube kernels and set them aside, saying:”
‘This is my father, and this is my father’s father’—monks, the fathers of that man would not come to an end, even if this great earth were to reach its exhaustion and destruction. Why is that?
Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
"No prior limit is discerned for beings who, obstructed by ignorance and fettered by craving, have wandered and transmigrated.
Thus, monks, for a very long time you have experienced suffering, experienced what is fierce, experienced calamity, and increased the charnel ground.
To this extent, monks, it is enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena; it is enough to become dispassionate toward them; it is enough to be liberated from them."
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 15.3 (SN 15.3, PTS SN ii 179) 1.
First Chapter
The Assu Sutta.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.”
No beginning point is discerned for beings who, obstructed by ignorance and fettered by craving, run on and wander through the cycle of existence.

What do you think, monks: which is more, the tears you have shed while running on and wandering through this long stretch of time—weeping and crying out at union with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant—or [the earth]?
“Is the pus that has flowed and trickled greater, or the water in the four great oceans?
“Venerable sir, as we understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this alone that is greater:
the amount of unpleasant associations and separations from the pleasant that we have experienced while wandering and transmigrating through this long course of time.”

“The tears that have flowed and streamed from you while weeping and wailing as you wandered and transmigrated through this long stretch of time—even this is more than the water in the four great oceans.
“Excellent, excellent, monks! It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me in this way.
Monks, it is precisely this that is more abundant: the tears that have flowed and streamed from you while weeping and wailing as you wandered and transmigrated through this long stretch of time.”
The tears that have flowed and streamed from you while weeping and wailing due to association with the unpleasant and dissociation from the pleasant exceed the water in the four great oceans.
For a long time, monks, you have experienced the death of a mother.

As you have experienced the death of your mothers, encountering the unpleasant and being separated from the pleasant, weeping and wailing, the tears that flowed and streamed forth exceed the water in the four great oceans.
For a long time, monks, you have experienced the death of your fathers...
[and so on] ...you have experienced the death of your brothers...
The death of a sister was experienced...
the death of a son was experienced...
the death of a daughter was experienced...
The misfortune of relatives has been experienced...
the misfortune of wealth has been experienced.
For a long time, monks, you have experienced the misfortune of illness; while experiencing that misfortune of illness, you—
The tears that have flowed and streamed from those weeping and wailing due to association with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant—
even this exceeds the water in the four great oceans. And why is that?
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning….
To such an extent, bhikkhus, is it enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them.
The third.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 15.4 (SN 15.4, PTS SN ii 180) 1. First Chapter: The Milk Discourse (Khīrasutta) “Bhikkhus, just as when milk is being churned with a churning-stick, at first the cream appears; from the cream, curd; from the curd, butter; from the butter, ghee; and from the ghee, the scum of ghee. And whatever is of the nature to arise in that milk, that has arisen; whatever is of the nature to appear in that milk, that has appeared; whatever is of the nature to come to be in that milk, that has come to be. “So too, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years, one of two fruits is to be expected: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. “What do you think, bhikkhus? Would it not be reasonable for a noble disciple to have confidence in the Teacher thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One’? “Yes, venerable sir. “It is because he has developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years that it is reasonable for him to have such confidence in the Teacher. “What do you think, bhikkhus? Would it not be reasonable for a noble disciple to have confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise’? “Yes, venerable sir. “It is because he has developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years that it is reasonable for him to have such confidence in the Dhamma. “What do you think, bhikkhus? Would it not be reasonable for a noble disciple to have confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world’? “Yes, venerable sir. “It is because he has developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years that it is reasonable for him to have such confidence in the Saṅgha. “What do you think, bhikkhus? Would it not be reasonable for a noble disciple to possess the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped at, leading to concentration? “Yes, venerable sir. “It is because he has developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years that it is reasonable for him to possess such virtues dear to the noble ones. “What do you think, bhikkhus? Would it not be reasonable for a noble disciple to possess the view of a noble disciple—the kind of view that is possessed by a noble disciple, which is founded upon and based upon the Dhamma, and leads to the utter destruction of suffering? “Yes, venerable sir. “It is because he has developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years that it is reasonable for him to possess such a view of a noble disciple. “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five factors, he is called a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination.

[The Buddha then repeated the entire sequence, substituting “eight years” for “seven years,” “nine years,” “ten years,” “eleven years,” “twelve years,” “thirteen years,” “fourteen years,” “fifteen years,” “sixteen years,” “seventeen years,” “eighteen years,” “nineteen years,” “twenty years,” “thirty years,” “forty years,” “fifty years,” “sixty years,” “seventy years,” “eighty years,” “ninety years,” and finally “a hundred years. “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five factors, he is called a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. [The Buddha then repeated the entire sequence, substituting “one year” for “a hundred years,” “two years,” “three years,” “four years,” “five years,” “six years,” “seven years,” “eight years,” “nine years,” “ten years,” “eleven years,” “twelve years,” “thirteen years,” “fourteen years,” “fifteen years,” “sixteen years,” “seventeen years,” “eighteen years,” “nineteen years,” “twenty years,” “thirty years,” “forty years,” “fifty years,” “sixty years,” “seventy years,” “eighty years,” “ninety years,” and finally “a hundred years. “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five factors, he is called a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. [The Buddha then repeated the entire sequence, substituting “one day” for “a hundred years,” “two days,” “three days,” “four days,” “five days,” “six days,” “seven days,” “eight days,” “nine days,” “ten days,” “eleven days,” “twelve days,” “thirteen days,” “fourteen days,” “fifteen days,” “sixteen days,” “seventeen days,” “eighteen days,” “nineteen days,” “twenty days,” “thirty days,” “forty days,” “fifty days,” “sixty days,” “seventy days,” “eighty days,” “ninety days,” and finally “a hundred days. “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five factors, he is called a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. [The Buddha then repeated the entire sequence, substituting “one night” for “a hundred days,” “two nights,” “three nights,” “four nights,” “five nights,” “six nights,” “seven nights,” “eight nights,” “nine nights,” “ten nights,” “eleven nights,” “twelve nights,” “thirteen nights,” “fourteen nights,” “fifteen nights,” “sixteen nights,” “seventeen nights,” “eighteen nights,” “nineteen nights,” “twenty nights,” “thirty nights,” “forty nights,” “fifty nights,” “sixty nights,” “seventy nights,” “eighty nights,” “ninety nights,” and finally “a hundred nights. “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five factors, he is called a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. [The Buddha then repeated the entire sequence, substituting “one watch of the night” for “a hundred nights,” “two watches of the night,” “three watches of the night,” “four watches of the night,” “five watches of the night,” “six watches of the night,” “seven watches of the night,” “eight watches of the night,” “nine watches of the night,” “ten watches of the night,” “eleven watches of the night,” “twelve watches of the night,” “thirteen watches of the night,” “fourteen watches of the night,” “fifteen watches of the night,” “sixteen watches of the night,” “seventeen watches of the night,” “eighteen watches of the night,” “nineteen watches of the night,” “twenty watches of the night,” “thirty watches of the night,” “forty watches of the night,” “fifty watches of the night,” “sixty watches of the night,” “seventy watches of the night,” “eighty watches of the night,” “ninety watches of the night,” and finally “a hundred watches of the night. “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five factors, he is called a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. At Sāvatthī. “Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.”
"What do you think, monks? Which is more: the mother’s milk that you have drunk while wandering and transmigrating through this long course of time, or the water in the four great oceans?

"Venerable sir, as we understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is the mother’s milk that we have drunk while wandering and transmigrating through this long course of time that is far more, and not the water in the four great oceans."
“...the water in the great oceans.
“Excellent, excellent, monks! It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me in this way.
Monks, it is indeed more than that—the mother’s milk you have drunk while wandering and transmigrating throughout this long stretch of time—that is more than the water in the four great oceans.”
For what reason?
Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning...
[as before] ...enough for liberation.
The Fourth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 15.5 (SN 15.5, PTS SN ii 181) 1.
First Chapter
The Mountain Discourse.
The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, in a certain monastery...
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“How long, venerable sir, is an eon?
“An eon, bhikkhu, is long.
It is not easy to calculate it as ‘this many years,’ or ‘this many hundreds of years,’ or ‘this many thousands of years,’ or ‘this many hundreds of thousands of years.’”
“But, venerable sir, is it possible to give a simile?
“It is possible, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said.
“Suppose, bhikkhu, there were a great mountain of rock—a solid mass of stone, one yojana in length, one yojana in width, and one yojana in height, without cracks or fissures, a single solid block.
Suppose, monk, a man were to wipe that great mountain of rock once every hundred years with a cloth from Kāsi.
By this means, monk, that great mountain of rock would sooner be worn away and brought to an end than an eon.
So long, monk, is an eon.
"Thus, monk, throughout long eons, many eons have been passed, many hundreds of eons have been passed, many thousands of eons have been passed, many hundreds of thousands of eons have been passed.
And why is that? Because this saṃsāra, monk, has no discoverable beginning."
“The prior limit... [as before] ...
To this extent, bhikkhu, it is indeed enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them.
The fifth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 15.6 (SN 15.6, PTS SN ii 182) 1. First Chapter: The Chapter on the Simile of the Mustard Seed The Discourse on the Mustard Seed “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a blind tortoise that emerged from the depths of the great ocean once every hundred years. And suppose there were a yoke with a single hole in it, tossed about by the winds upon the surface of the great ocean. What do you think, bhikkhus, would that blind tortoise, emerging from the depths of the great ocean once every hundred years, ever thrust its neck through that yoke with a single hole? “It would not be easy, venerable sir. “Even less so, bhikkhus, is the acquisition of human birth. For this, bhikkhus, is the long night of saṃsāra. For this, bhikkhus, is the long course of saṃsāra. For this, bhikkhus, is the long round of saṃsāra. “In this long night of saṃsāra, bhikkhus, you have undergone much suffering, experienced much suffering, and felt much suffering. You have undergone much death, experienced much death, and felt much death. You have undergone much falling away, experienced much falling away, and felt much falling away. You have undergone much birth, experienced much birth, and felt much birth. “Enough, bhikkhus, of heaping up more karma. Enough of accumulating more karma. For, bhikkhus, when karma has been done and accumulated, its result will be experienced here and now, or in the next life, or in subsequent lives. Therefore, bhikkhus, abandon unwholesome states; cultivate wholesome states; be pure in conduct; be perfect in virtue; be restrained according to the Pātimokkha; be endowed with a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing; train yourselves in the higher training in morality, the higher training in concentration, and the higher training in wisdom. “Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a householder or a householder’s son, rich, wealthy, and affluent, possessing abundant gold and silver, abundant treasures and granaries, abundant wealth and property, and many wives, sons, daughters, and servants. He had a single precious gem, worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. Then, having gone on a journey to some foreign land, he would entrust his family with that gem, saying: ‘This, my dear family, is our sole treasure, our sole wealth, our sole property. Guard it well; do not let it be lost. “Then, after some time, that householder or householder’s son would return from his journey to that foreign land. On returning, he would ask his family: ‘My dear family, where is that gem? They would reply: ‘We do not know, master. Then, having struck them with his fist, he would say: ‘Fools! You have lost our sole treasure, our sole wealth, our sole property! “Now, bhikkhus, what do you think? Would those people, being struck with his fist, feel pain because of that? “Yes, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, even though they might feel pain because of being struck with his fist, that is nothing compared to the suffering they would experience if they were to lose that gem. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that gem was their sole treasure, their sole wealth, their sole property. So too, bhikkhus, in this long night of saṃsāra... [as above]... Therefore, bhikkhus, abandon unwholesome states; cultivate wholesome states; be pure in conduct; be perfect in virtue; be restrained according to the Pātimokkha; be endowed with a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing; train yourselves in the higher training in morality, the higher training in concentration, and the higher training in wisdom.”
The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sat down to one side. Sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"Bhante, how long, indeed, is an eon?"
“Bhikkhu, an eon is long.
It is not easy to calculate it as ‘this many years’ … or ‘this many hundreds of thousands of years.
“But, Bhante, is it possible to provide a simile?”
“It is possible, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.
“Suppose, bhikkhu, there were an iron city, a yojana in length, a yojana in width, and a yojana in height, filled with mustard seeds packed together in balls.

Then, at the end of every hundred years, a man were to remove a single mustard seed from it. [In this way, the exhaustion of that heap would be quicker than the attainment of arahantship by one who possesses such qualities].”
"Monk, by this method, that great heap of mustard seeds would more quickly reach exhaustion and depletion than an eon.
So long, monk, is an eon.
And of such long eons, monk, many eons have been passed, many hundreds of eons have been passed, many thousands of eons have been passed, many hundreds of thousands of eons have been passed."
For what reason?
Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning...
[as before] ...it is enough to be liberated.
Sixth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 15.7 (SN 15.7, PTS SN ii 182) 1.
First Chapter
The Discourse on Disciples.
The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and as they were sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“How many eons, Bhante, have passed and gone by?
“Many eons, bhikkhus, have passed and gone by.
They are not easy to count:”
‘So many eons,’ or ‘so many hundreds of eons,’ or ‘so many thousands of eons,’ or ‘so many hundreds of thousands of eons.
“But, Bhante, is it possible to provide a simile?
“It is possible, monks,” the Blessed One said.
“Suppose, monks, there were four disciples with a lifespan of a hundred years,
living for a hundred years. If they were to recollect a hundred thousand eons each day, a hundred thousand eons each day—

even if those eons were not yet fully recollected by them— those four disciples, with a lifespan of a hundred years, living for a hundred years, would pass away at the end of that hundred-year period.”
In this way, monks, many eons have passed away and gone by.
They are not easy to calculate, such that one could say:
"There were this many eons," or "this many hundreds of eons," or "this many thousands of eons," or "this many hundreds of thousands of eons."
For what reason?
Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning...
[as before] ...enough for you to be liberated."
Seventh.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 15.8 (SN 15.8, PTS SN ii 183) 1.
First Chapter (Paṭhamavagga)
The Gaṅgā Sutta:
At Rājagaha, the Blessed One was staying in the Bamboo Grove.
Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, how many eons (*kappa*), indeed, have passed and gone by?
"Brahmin, many eons have passed and gone by."
“They cannot easily be calculated as ‘this many eons,’ or ‘this many hundreds of eons,’ or ‘this many thousands of eons,’ or ‘this many hundreds of thousands of eons. “But,
Master Gotama, is it possible to provide a simile?”
“It is possible, brahmin,” the Blessed One said.
“Suppose, brahmin, there were the sand of the river Ganges from where it originates until where it enters the great ocean; it would not be easy to count that sand, saying:

‘There are this many grains of sand,’ or ‘there are this many hundreds of grains of sand,’ or ‘there are this many thousands of grains of sand,’ or ‘there are this many hundreds of thousands of grains of sand.’”
"Even more numerous than that, brahmin, are the eons that have passed away and gone by.
They are not easy to calculate, saying:
'there were this many eons,' or 'this many hundreds of eons,' or 'this many thousands of eons,' or 'this many hundreds of thousands of eons.'"
For what reason?
Brahmin, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A prior limit is not discerned for beings who, obstructed by ignorance and fettered by craving, wander and transmigrate.
“Thus, brahmin, for a long time suffering has been experienced, intense suffering has been experienced, calamity has been experienced, and the charnel ground has been enlarged.
To this extent, brahmin, it is indeed enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, and enough to be liberated from them.
When this was said, that brahmin addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The eighth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 15.9 (SN 15.9, PTS SN ii 184) 1. First Chapter: The Chapter on the Six Sense Bases The Discourse on the Staff "Bhikkhus, just as when a man with good sight, having taken a staff, examines his own body, so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses the noble wisdom of insight into phenomena examines this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities: 'In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys; heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; bowels, entrails, gorge, dung; bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine. Just as if, bhikkhus, there were a bag with an opening at both ends full of various kinds of grain, such as hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, millet, and white rice, and a man with good sight, having opened it, were to examine them: 'This is hill rice, this is red rice, these are beans, these are peas, this is millet, this is white rice'; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses the noble wisdom of insight into phenomena examines this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities... Just as if, bhikkhus, there were a pit full of worms, and a man with good sight, having lowered himself into it, were to examine them: 'These are earthworms'; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses the noble wisdom of insight into phenomena examines this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities... Just as if, bhikkhus, there were a bowl of ghee or oil, and a man with good sight, having uncovered it, were to examine it: 'This is ghee or oil'; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses the noble wisdom of insight into phenomena examines this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities... Just as if, bhikkhus, there were a jar of honey, and a man with good sight, having uncovered it, were to examine it: 'This is honey'; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses the noble wisdom of insight into phenomena examines this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities... Just as if, bhikkhus, there were a jar of blood, and a man with good sight, having uncovered it, were to examine it: 'This is blood'; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses the noble wisdom of insight into phenomena examines this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities... Just as if, bhikkhus, there were a water-jar full of water, and a man with good sight, having uncovered it, were to examine it: 'This is water'; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses the noble wisdom of insight into phenomena examines this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities: 'In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys; heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; bowels, entrails, gorge, dung; bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine. When he thus examines this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities, he does not regard it as 'I' or 'mine' or 'my self. He understands: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple experiences revulsion toward form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: 'It is liberated. He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.'"
At Sāvatthī. “Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.”
"Just as, monks, a stick thrown into the air falls now on its base, now on its middle, and now on its tip;
even so, monks, beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, running and wandering on, go from this world to the other world and come from the other world back to this world.
For what reason? [Because of their ignorance and craving]."
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning...
[as before] ...enough for you to be disenchanted, enough to become dispassionate, enough to be liberated. The ninth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 15.10 (SN 15.10, PTS SN ii 185) 1. First Chapter: The Discourse on Persons (Puggalasutta) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is bound by both ends; the person who is bound by one end; the person who is liberated in both ways; and the person who is liberated by wisdom. And how, monks, is one a person bound by both ends? Here, a certain person is not devoid of lust, hatred, and delusion regarding the past, and he is not devoid of lust, hatred, and delusion regarding the future. This, monks, is called a person bound by both ends. And how, monks, is one a person bound by one end? Here, a certain person is not devoid of lust, hatred, and delusion regarding the past, but he is devoid of lust, hatred, and delusion regarding the future. This, monks, is called a person bound by one end. And how, monks, is one a person liberated in both ways? Here, a certain person has, through the destruction of the taints, realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells therein. This, monks, is called a person liberated in both ways. And how, monks, is one a person liberated by wisdom? Here, a certain person has, through the destruction of the five lower fetters, been reborn spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and will attain final Nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. This, monks, is called a person liberated by wisdom. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning …” [as above] …

“Monks, for a single person wandering and transmigrating for an eon, there might be such a great heap of bones, such a pile of bones, such a mass of bones, as this mountain Vepulla, if there were one to collect them and that collection were not lost. Why is that?
Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning…”
“Enough with being liberated!
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
“In a single eon,
the accumulation of bones of a single person could become a heap equal to a mountain.”
Thus it was said by the Great Seer.
And this great mountain Vepulla has been described.
To the north of Vulture Peak,
the mountain of Magadha,
there where the Noble Truths [were taught].
One sees with right wisdom:
suffering, the arising of suffering,
and the transcendence of suffering.
And the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the stilling of suffering—
he is one for whom there are at most seven more births.
Having run the course, a person becomes an ender of suffering through the destruction of all fetters.
The tenth.
The first chapter.
Its summary verse:
Grass and wood, earth,
tears and milk, mountains; mustard seeds,
disciples, and the Ganges.
"The rod and the person.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 15.11 (SN 15.11, PTS SN ii 186) 2.
Second Chapter.
The Discourse to Duggata.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
There, [the Blessed One said: …pe…
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned for beings who, obstructed by ignorance and fettered by craving, wander and roam on.
Bhikkhus, whatever you may see there as one who is miserable and poorly off, you should reach the conclusion: [this is the result of past deeds].”
‘We too have experienced such things throughout this long stretch of time.
For what reason?
… [as before] … To this extent, bhikkhus, it is indeed enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them.”
First.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 15.12 (SN 15.12, PTS SN ii 186) 2.
Second Chapter
The Discourse on Happiness.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning …” [as above] …
“Monks, when you see someone who is happy and well-provided for, you should come to the conclusion: ‘We too have experienced such things over this long course of time.

For what reason? Because we have all been subject to birth, aging, and death; to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Since we have all been subject to these, it is reasonable that we too have experienced such happiness and prosperity over this long course of time.”
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned ... [as before] ...
enough to be liberated.”
The Second [Discourse].
Saṃyutta Nikāya 15.13 (SN 15.13, PTS SN ii 187). Chapter Two.
The Second Subchapter.
The Discourse on the Thirty:
At Rājagaha, he was staying in the Bamboo Grove.
Then, thirty bhikkhus from Pāvā—all forest-dwellers, all alms-food eaters, and all wearers of rag-robes—approached him.
All were wearers of the three robes and all were still bound by fetters; they approached the Blessed One, and having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
“These thirty bhikkhus from Pāvā are all forest-dwellers, all alms-collectors, all wearers of rag-robes, all possessors of the three robes, yet all are still bound by the fetters.
What if I were to teach them the Dhamma in such a way that, even on this very seat, their minds would be liberated from the taints through non-clinging?
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.
What do you think, monks, which is more: that which is yours in this long course of time—”
"Between the blood that has flowed and been shed from the heads of those who have run and wandered through the cycle of rebirth,
and the water in the four great oceans—
which is greater? "Venerable sir, as we understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, this very [blood], venerable sir, is far more."
“The blood that has flowed and been shed from our heads as we have wandered and transmigrated through this long stretch of time is more than the water in the four great oceans.
“Excellent, excellent, monks! It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me in this way.”

“Monks, this alone is more: the clear blood that has flowed and been shed from your heads as you have wandered and transmigrated through this long stretch of time, than the water in the four great oceans.
For a long time, monks, as you were born as cattle and had your heads cut off, the clear blood that flowed and was shed is more than the water in the four great oceans.”
For a long time, monks, when you were buffaloes, having had your heads cut off, clear blood flowed from you...
For a long time, monks, when you were sheep... for a long time, monks, when you were goats...
Of a hundred deer who have become deer...
of a hundred chickens who have become chickens...
of a hundred pigs who have become pigs...
For a long time, monks, you have had clear blood flow from your heads after being seized and beheaded for being village-robbers.
For a long time, monks, you have had clear blood flow from your heads after being seized and beheaded for being highwaymen.
For a long time, monks, you have had clear blood flow from your heads after being seized and beheaded for being adulterers—more than there is water in the four great oceans.
For what reason?
Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning...
[as before] ...enough for liberation.
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The bhikkhus were satisfied and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of thirty bhikkhus from Pāvā were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Third.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 15.18 (SN 15.18, PTS SN ii 190) 2. Second Chapter: On Sons (Puttasutta) "Monks, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? They are the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, do not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging, I say that those ascetics or brahmins are not fully enlightened. And why is that? Because, monks, it is by understanding as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging that a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One claims supreme enlightenment. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We will understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves."
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was staying … “Monks, it is not easy to find a being who has not previously been one’s son … it is enough to be liberated.”
The Eighth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 15.19 (SN 15.19, PTS SN ii 190) 2.
Second Chapter (Dutiyavagga)
The Dhītusutta.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
"Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning."
No beginning point is discerned for beings who, obstructed by ignorance and fettered by craving, run on and wander through the cycle of existence.
Monks, it is not easy to find a being who has not previously been one's daughter during this long stretch of time. And why is that?
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.
For such a long time, bhikkhus, you have experienced suffering, experienced anguish, experienced disaster; the charnel ground has been enlarged.
"To this extent, monks, it is indeed enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them.
Thus was the ninth [discourse]. Saṁyutta Nikāya 15.20 (SN 15.20, PTS SN ii 190).
2. The Second Chapter:
The Sutta on Mount Vepulla.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving."
In the past, monks, this Vepulla mountain received the designation ‘Pācīnavaṃsa.
At that time, monks, humans were known by the designation ‘Tivaras.
The lifespan of the Tivara humans was forty thousand years.
“Bhikkhus, the Tivaras take four days to climb Mount Pācīnavaṃsa and four days to descend from it.
At that time, bhikkhus, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had appeared in the world.
For the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was a pair of chief disciples named Vidhura and Sañjīva, a most auspicious pair.”
Behold, monks, how this mountain’s name has vanished, how those people have passed away, and how that Blessed One has attained final nibbāna.
Thus, monks, are conditioned phenomena impermanent;
thus, monks, are conditioned phenomena unstable.
"Thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are not to be relied upon.
To this extent, monks, it is indeed enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them.
Once in the past, monks, this mountain Vepulla acquired the designation 'Vaṅkaka' (the Crooked)."
Now at that time, monks, the designation “Rohitassas” arose for human beings.
The life span of the Rohitassa humans, monks, was thirty thousand years.
The Rohitassa humans, monks, would ascend Mount Vaṅkaka in three days and descend in three days.
Now at that time, monks, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had arisen in the world.
The Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of chief disciples named Bhiyyosuttara, a most excellent and auspicious pair.
Behold, monks, how even the name of this mountain has vanished, those people have passed away, and that Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna.
"Thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are impermanent...
[as before] ...enough for liberation.
Once upon a time, monks, this Vepulla mountain had the designation 'Supassa'."
At that time, monks, the common designation for human beings arose as “Suppiyas.
The lifespan of the Suppiya humans, monks, was twenty thousand years.
The Suppiya humans, monks, would ascend Mount Supassa in two days and descend in two days.
At that time, monks, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had appeared in the world.
The Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of chief disciples named Tissa and Bhāradvāja, a most auspicious pair.
Behold, monks, how even the name of this mountain has vanished, those people have passed away, and that Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna.
"Thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are unstable...
enough for liberation."
But now, monks, the designation ‘Vepulla’ has arisen for this Vepulla mountain.
And now, monks, the designation ‘Māgadha’ has arisen for these people.
For the people of Magadha, monks, the lifespan is short, limited, and brief.
Whoever lives long, monks, lives for a hundred years or a little more.
Monks, the people of Magadha ascend Mount Vepulla in a short moment and descend from it in a short moment.
But now, monks, I have arisen in the world as an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Moreover, monks, I have a pair of disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna, a supreme and auspicious pair.
There will come a time, monks, when this very name of this mountain shall disappear, when these people shall pass away, and when I too shall attain final Nibbāna.
Thus, monks, are conditioned phenomena impermanent.
"Thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are unstable;
thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are unreliable.
To this extent, monks, it is sufficient to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, sufficient to become dispassionate toward them, and sufficient to be liberated from them."
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
“The Eastern Pillar of the Tivaras...”
Vaṅkaka belongs to the Rohitas,
Supassa to the Suppiyas,
and Vepulla to the Māgadhas.
Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena,
subject to the nature of arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease.
The subsiding of these is bliss.
Tenth. The Second Chapter.
Its summary verse:
The one in distress and the one in happiness,
thirty [verses] on mother and father.
The brother, the sister, the son,
and the daughter [visited] Vepulla Mountain.
The *Anamatagga-saṃyutta* is complete.
